title: The Immortal Game: initiative against material
outcomes: Finds the engine's first choice at seven decision points of a famous game (the last two lie in the usual published finish), before seeing the move that was played
Says which offers in the game were practical gambles and which was a forced mate, naming the engine depth behind each statement
Names the core skills that decided the finish and the two captures where the game turned

steps.text:
**London, 1851.** In the standard account, Adolf Anderssen had White against Lionel Kieseritzky in a casual game beside the London tournament. In the usual score he gives up a bishop, both rooks and the queen, and still mates; the last moves may never have been played on the board.
You will choose White's moves, and two Black moves. Engine remarks name their search depth: evidence, not proof.

steps.caption: Anderssen (White) against Kieseritzky (Black). Step through the first ten moves.

line.say: White opens with the king's pawn.
Black copies.
White offers the f-pawn: the King's Gambit.
Black takes the pawn.
The bishop looks at f7.
Black's queen comes out with check.
White's king steps to f1.
Black puts a pawn where the bishop attacks it.
White takes it.
Black develops a knight and attacks the e4 pawn.
The knight attacks the queen.
The queen retreats along the h-file.
White defends the e4 pawn with the d-pawn.
Black's knight goes to h5.
White's knight goes to h4.
The queen steps to g5.
The knight lands on f5, attacking g7.
Black attacks the bishop with a pawn.
White advances the g-pawn, attacking the knight on h5.
The knight returns to f6 and attacks the g4 pawn.

claims.statement: After 3.Bc4 the bishop attacks f7.
After 4...b5 the bishop on c4 attacks the pawn on b5.
After 5...Nf6 the knight attacks e4.
After 6.Nf3 the knight attacks the queen on h4.
After 7.d3 the d-pawn defends e4.
After 9.Nf5 the knight attacks g7.
After 9...c6 the pawn attacks the bishop on b5.
After 10.g4 the pawn attacks the knight on h5.
After 10...Nf6 Black attacks the g4 pawn twice (knight and queen).

line.say: Black takes the bishop. At depth 16 the engine prefers 11...h5 and rates this capture over a pawn and a half lower.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's first choice for Black is h5.
At depth 16 the engine rates cxb5 at least one and a half pawns lower than h5.

steps.caption: White to move after 11...cxb5. White has just lost a bishop.

line.say: The pawn attacks the queen.
The queen steps to g6.
The pawn attacks it again.
The queen goes back to g5.
Now f4 is attacked twice and defended once.
The knight retreats to g8.
The bishop takes the pawn back and attacks the queen.
The queen steps to f6.

claims.statement: After 13.h5 the pawn attacks the queen on g6.
After 14.Qf3 White attacks f4 twice (queen and bishop).
After 14.Qf3 Black defends f4 once (queen).
After 15.Bxf4 the bishop attacks the queen on g5.

line.say: The knight comes out and blocks the queen's line to b2.
Black's bishop attacks the rook on g1.
The knight jumps to d5 and attacks the queen.
The queen takes b2 and attacks the rook on a1.

claims.statement: After 16...Bc5 the bishop attacks the rook on g1.
After 17.Nd5 the knight attacks the queen on f6.
After 17...Qxb2 the queen attacks the rook on a1.

line.say: The famous bishop move. At depth 16 the engine ranks d4, Rd1 and Re1 ahead of it by over a pawn and a half.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's first choices are d4, Re1 and Rd1, within four tenths of a pawn of each other.
At depth 16 the engine rates Bd6 at least one and a half pawns lower than its first choice.

steps.caption: In Kieseritzky's report Black played 18...Bxg1; some books list 18...Qxa1+ first and reach the same position after move 20. White has now lost a bishop and a rook. White to move.

line.say: The pawn closes the long diagonal, so g7 loses its guard. At depth 16 the engine prefers 19.Re1 or 19.Qd1.
Black takes the second rook.
The king goes to e2.
Black's knight goes to a6. Kieseritzky's published report stops after 20.Ke2; the finish that follows is the usual continuation and may never have been played.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's first choices are Re1 and Qd1, within six tenths of a pawn of each other.
At depth 16 the engine rates e5 at least one and a half pawns lower than its first choice.
At depth 20 the engine rates White ahead by two pawns or more here.
Before e5 Black's queen defends g7.
After e5 nothing of Black's defends g7.
A black queen stands on a1, where White's rook stood.
A black bishop stands on g1, where White's other rook stood.

steps.caption: After 21.Nxg7+. Black to move, in check.

line.say: Black has one legal reply.

claims.statement: Black's king is in check.
Kd8 is Black's only legal move.

line.say: Black has two legal replies. Taking the queen leaves e7 attacked twice and defended once. This is the reply in the usual score.

claims.statement: Black has two legal replies: Ne7 and Nxf6.
After Nxf6 only the king defends e7.
After Nxf6 White still attacks e7 twice.

line.say: Be7 is checkmate.

claims.statement: Be7 is checkmate.

steps.prompt: Before the summary: which of White's offers (11.Rg1, 18.Bd6, 22.Qf6+) would you call a practical gamble, and which a forced mate? Which two Black captures turned the game?

steps.text: **What decided it?** *Types of sacrifice*: 11.Rg1 (slightly worse for White, depth 22) and 18.Bd6 (at least 1.5 pawns below the first choices, depth 16) were practical gambles; 22.Qf6+ was sound, a forced mate (depth 16). *Tangible superiority before attacking*: two White minor pieces out against one at move 11. *Searching for a forced mate* and *deflection* finished it. Black's captures 11...cxb5 and 18...Bxg1 each rate at least 1.5 pawns below the engine's choice (depth 16).

steps.prompt: Which moment would you have missed: the bishop offer, the pawn pushes that hit the queen, the knight move to c3, Black's choice of capture, or the queen sacrifice? What will you look at first next time?

sources: Game score, checked against each other and replayed move by move in python-chess: Wikipedia 'Immortal Game' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immortal_Game, full score, casual status, note that the last moves may not have been played on the board); E. Lasker, Common Sense in Chess (public domain, sources/raw/emlasker_common-sense_archive.txt, descriptive notation in OCR text, converted by hand); logicalchess.com game page G_0053 (PGN to move 20, notes Kieseritzky's report in La Regence lacks the final combination); jaced.com 'The Immortal Game' (full score; a few moves in a different order that reaches the same position). The order of moves 18 to 20 differs between sources: Lasker has 18...Qxa1+ 19.Ke2 Bxg1 20.e5 [V, read in the OCR text]; Wikipedia, logicalchess.com and the La Regence list have 18...Bxg1 19.e5 Qxa1+ 20.Ke2 [S, as relayed by a reviewer, not re-read here]; python-chess confirms both orders reach the same position after move 20 [V]. Whether moves 21 to 23 were played on the board is uncertain [S].

chessgames.com game page (casual game, London, 21 June 1851, 1-0; metadata and the note 'sac: 11.Rg1' only) and ChessBase '50 games you should know' (date and place only): read through a page-summarising fetch tool, so move lists were taken from the pages above and replayed.
Engine: Stockfish 19 lite, single thread, depths named in each claim (content/items/lesson-fg-immortal.json and this lesson's board claims).
